title: Removal and Dismantling of Mechanical Components and Parts

lessons.title: Removing parts safely in the workplace
lessons.html:
Your role

In the workplace you help the mechanic remove and dismantle parts such as water pumps, alternators, starters, wheels, linkage arms, PTO shafts and hydraulic cylinders. You must work safely, carefully and in order, so that nothing is lost or damaged.

Before you start

  1. Get the job card and ask the mechanic what to remove.
  2. Look at the workshop manual pages for the job.
  3. Make the tractor safe: level ground, implements down, handbrake on, wheels chocked, key out, tag on the steering wheel.
  4. Disconnect the battery negative lead if you are working near wiring or the starter.
  5. Let the engine and exhaust cool.

Prepare your area

  • Clean the outside of the part with a brush or degreaser so dirt does not fall in.
  • Have trays, bags, labels and a marker ready.
  • Put a drip tray under the part if it holds oil or coolant.

Removing the part

  • Take photos before and during removal.
  • Label every wire and hose.
  • Put bolts in a labelled bag or tray. Different bolts can have different lengths.
  • Cap hoses and open holes.
  • Support heavy parts with a jack, crane or helper before taking out the last bolts.

Lifting

Heavy parts like wheels and cylinders can crush hands and feet. Use lifting equipment. Keep fingers out of pinch points. Never stand under a part hanging on a crane.

Stuck bolts

Spray penetrating oil and wait. Use a ring spanner or six-point socket. Do not use heat without the mechanic's permission. If a bolt is about to break, stop and ask.

lessons.title: Dismantling and laying out parts
lessons.html:
Dismantling on the bench

Once a part is removed, it may need to be taken apart so the mechanic can check it. For example, a water pump, a hydraulic cylinder or a hub.

Work in a clean place

  • Clean the bench first. Put down clean paper or a mat.
  • Clean the outside of the part before opening it.
  • Use the right tools: pullers, bearing separators, snap ring pliers, soft-face hammer.
  • Use a vice with soft jaws for finished parts.

Keep parts in order

Lay parts out on the bench in the order you remove them, from left to right. This makes putting them back easier. Keep shims, washers and small parts in labelled containers. Never mix parts from two jobs.

Springs and snap rings

Some parts have springs under pressure. They can fly out and hurt your eyes. Wear safety glasses. Use the correct tool to hold the spring while you remove the snap ring. Ask the mechanic if you are not sure.

Bearings and seals

Use a puller or press to remove bearings and gears. Do not hit bearings with a steel hammer. Keep old seals and gaskets so the mechanic can compare them with the new ones, then dispose of them.

Cleaning parts

Clean parts in the parts washer with the approved cleaner. Wear gloves and glasses. Do not use petrol to clean parts; it can catch fire. Dry parts with clean rags or low-pressure air, pointing it away from people.

Report what you see

Look at each part as you clean it. Tell the mechanic if you see:

  • cracks or broken pieces
  • worn or broken gear teeth
  • rough or noisy bearings
  • scoring or deep scratches
  • metal pieces in the oil

Finishing

Cover parts to keep dust off. Write on the job card what you removed and dismantled. Put waste oil and old parts in the right bins.

Key points

  • Make the tractor safe before removing anything.
  • Photograph, label and bag parts and bolts.
  • Lay parts out in order on a clean bench.
  • Wear safety glasses when removing springs and snap rings.
  • Never clean parts with petrol, and report any damage you see.
